    "description": "Decode 1D barcodes and QR codes from images into payload text with format detection, orientation handling, and honest confidence reporting for damaged codes.",
    "body": "Barcode and QR Scanning Category: Perception | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A barcode or QR code is a machine-readable string with a strict geometry. This skill covers locating candidate code regions in an image, detecting the symbology, decoding the payload, and reporting confidence honestly — including the case where a damaged or partially occluded code decodes to a wrong-but-checksum-valid result. When to Use Use when an image contains barcodes or QR codes whose payload drives a decision — inventory labels, ticket validation, payment codes, hardware serials. Do not treat a successful decode as ground truth without the symbology checksum; low-quality images decode to plausible wrong values more often than they fail outright. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The image containing one or more codes | | | | No | Crop to scan when the code location is known | | | | No | Restrict detection to given symbologies | Procedure 1. Locate candidate code regions before decoding — finder patterns for QR codes, quiet-zone and bar geometry for 1D symbologies. 2. Detect the symbology from the located region rather than trying every decoder and taking the first success. 3. Normalize the region — deskew, binarize, correct perspective — before attempting the decode. 4. Decode the payload and verify the symbology checksum; reject codes that fail their check digit. 5. Report per-code confidence and symbology together with the payload, and flag damaged regions explicitly. 6. Bound the work: cap the number of regions examined per image so pathological images cannot stall the pipeline. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Decoded payloads with symbology and checksum status | | | | Located code regions in image coordinates | | | | Regions that failed to decode, with reasons | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Wrong but valid decodes | Damaged codes decode to checksum-plausible wrong values | Flag low-confidence and damaged regions | | Missed codes | Codes at angles or small scale are not located | Use rotation-tolerant, multi-scale region detection | | Unbounded scanning | Pathological images stall detection | Cap regions and modules examined per image | | Payload taken as fact | A decoded string drives a decision unchecked | Verify the checksum and cross-check the expected format | | Symbology misclassification | The wrong decoder is applied to a region | Detect symbology from geometry before decoding | Security and Authority Boundary Decoded payloads are untrusted input. A QR code can encode a URL or instruction string; payloads must be validated against an expected format before being used to drive navigation, payment, or privileged actions. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The pyzbar barcode decoding library project page (https://pypi.org/project/pyzbar/). 2. The ZXing barcode image processing library GitHub repository (https://github.com/zxing/zxing). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it.     "description": "Parse X.509 certificates into structured fields — subject, issuer, validity, key usage — with explicit expiry checking and stated chain-validation boundaries.",
    "body": "Certificate Parsing Category: Perception | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A certificate is a signed claim about an identity, and most TLS mistakes come from reading one field of it in isolation. This skill parses a certificate into its material fields, checks validity windows and key usage against the operation at hand, and states clearly what a leaf certificate cannot tell you: whether its chain actually anchors to a trust store. When to Use Use when a workflow receives a certificate and needs its identity, expiry, or purpose fields — inventory of deployed certificates, pre-flight checks, incident triage of a TLS failure. Do not use field parsing as chain validation; a parsed, unexpired, purpose-matching certificate can still be untrusted, self-signed, or revoked. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The certificate to parse | | | | No | Clock to evaluate validity against; default is now | | | | No | Key usage the operation needs, such as server auth | Procedure 1. Decode PEM or DER into the certificate structure, reporting the encoding and size. 2. Extract the material fields — subject, issuer, serial, validity window, signature algorithm, key usage, subject alternative names. 3. Evaluate the validity window against the reference time and report days remaining, not just a boolean. 4. Check key usage and subject alternative names against the operation the certificate is being assessed for. 5. Read the file as text and preserve line numbers; do not trim or rewrite the raw input before parsing. 2. Skip blank lines and lines whose first non-space character is a hash; record them as ignored, not as errors. 3.
